# Save and restore a notebook

Suppose an application stores a notebook with sections, and each section holds
notes. One note appears in two sections. We want to save this graph to an RDS
file, restore its class references, and keep the shared note as one object.

The graph has three levels:

```text
Notebook
├── Section "Current" ── shared Note, draft Note
└── Section "Archive" ── shared Note
```

R saves the fields and references in this graph. The encoder records which
RObjC instances belong to which class, so the decoder can reconnect them to
class definitions available when the file is read.

```{r}
library(robjc)

Note <- RSObjectClass(
  "EncodingGuideNote", version = "1.0",
  public = list(
    title = NULL,     # character(1)
    priority = NULL,  # numeric(1)
    tags = NULL,      # character vector
    initialize = function(title, priority = 1, tags = character()) {
      super$initialize()
      self$title <- title
      self$priority <- priority
      self$tags <- tags
      invisible(self)
    }
  )
)

Section <- RSObjectClass(
  "EncodingGuideSection", version = "1.0",
  public = list(
    name = NULL,   # character(1)
    notes = NULL,  # list of Note objects
    initialize = function(name, notes = list()) {
      super$initialize()
      self$name <- name
      self$notes <- notes
      invisible(self)
    },
    objectsForEncoding = function() {
      c(super$objectsForEncoding(), self$notes)
    }
  )
)

Notebook <- RSObjectClass(
  "EncodingGuideNotebook", version = "1.0",
  public = list(
    sections = NULL,  # list of Section objects
    initialize = function(sections = list()) {
      super$initialize()
      self$sections <- sections
      invisible(self)
    },
    objectsForEncoding = function() {
      c(super$objectsForEncoding(), self$sections)
    }
  )
)
```

`Note` has only native R values, so it inherits the empty
`objectsForEncoding()` result from `RSObject`. `Section` returns its direct
`Note` children; `Notebook` returns its direct `Section` children. The notebook
does not need to list the notes itself: the encoder asks each section for its
children as it walks the graph.

## Native values and RObjC objects

`objectsForEncoding()` does **not** convert every field into an encoded value.
R's `saveRDS()` saves the contents of ordinary fields, including `numeric`,
`character`, `logical`, and their vectors. The encoder's job here is narrower:
it discovers RObjC objects whose **class references** need to be restored.

| Field in this example | What it contains | Return from `objectsForEncoding()`? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Note$title`, `Section$name` | Base R `character` | No; R saves the value. |
| `Note$priority`, `Note$tags` | Base R `numeric` and `character` vector | No; R saves the values. |
| `Section$notes` | A list of `Note` objects | Yes; return each `Note`, not the enclosing list. |
| `Notebook$sections` | A list of `Section` objects | Yes; return each `Section`. |

The distinction is the **field's value**, not its mathematical meaning. A
plain `2.5` is an R numeric value and needs no entry. An `RSNumber` object
containing `2.5` is an RObjC object; if stored in a field, return that object
so its class can be resolved. Likewise, a plain `"text"` is different from an
`RSString` object. A regular R list containing only atomic values does not
need to be returned. If a list contains RObjC objects, return those elements.

## Rules for listing and registering objects

- Override `objectsForEncoding()` when a class holds references to other RObjC
  objects. Return a **flat list** of direct children. For a list field such as
  `Section$notes`, append its elements; `list(self$notes)` would return a nested
  list rather than the notes themselves.
- Keep `NULL`, ordinary R values, and class generators out of the returned list.
  An object with no children returns `list()`. Include an optional child only
  when it is present.
- Include `super$objectsForEncoding()` so children owned by a superclass are
  retained. Do not include `self`: the encoder registers the current object
  before asking it for children. Repeated references and cycles are allowed.
- The encoder registers every returned child recursively and adds superclass
  metadata at `lockInstance()`. There is no separate call to register a child
  or its class.
- At read time, provide `class_map` entries for **every saved custom class ID**,
  including custom superclasses. Standard robjc classes are mapped automatically.

If a child is omitted, R still saves its field, but the decoder has no entry
with which to resolve that child's class reference.

## Choose the starting object (root)

A **root** is the object where the encoder starts walking; it does not mean the
`RSObject` base class. In this example the `notebook` variable is the root.
`robjc_save_rds(notebook, path)` saves that notebook as `__object__`, calls
`encodeObject(notebook)`, follows the sections and notes returned at each
level, and saves the resulting class metadata as `__robjc__`.

Choosing a section as the root would register that section and its notes, but
not an unrelated section elsewhere in the session. For several named roots,
`robjc_save()` saves the named objects and encodes each RObjC root. A manual
`encodeObject()` call only builds metadata in the encoder; it does not write an
RDS file. The save functions handle that step.

## Save the object graph

We build two sections that share one `Note` instance. `robjc_save_rds()` passes
the notebook root to the encoder and saves both the root and the metadata with
`saveRDS()`. The traversal reaches each section, then each note. When it sees
the shared note a second time, its visited-object record prevents a second
registration.

```{r}
# Build the graph. `notebook` is the one root we choose to save.
shared_note <- Note$new("Release checklist", 2.5, c("release", "shared"))
draft_note <- Note$new("Draft outline", 1, "draft")
notebook <- Notebook$new(list(
  Section$new("Current", list(shared_note, draft_note)),
  Section$new("Archive", list(shared_note))
))

# Save procedure: start encoding at `notebook` and write the RDS file.
path <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
robjc_save_rds(notebook, path)

# Verification only: inspect the raw payload and count registered instances.
# This readRDS() call does not resolve classes and is not part of normal loading.
payload <- readRDS(path)
entries <- payload$`__robjc__`$allEntriesAsList()
object_counts <- stats::setNames(
  vapply(entries, function(entry) as.integer(entry$value()$objects()$count()), integer(1)),
  vapply(entries, function(entry) entry$key()$value(), character(1))
)
expected_ids <- c(
  "EncodingGuideNotebook_1.0",
  "EncodingGuideSection_1.0",
  "EncodingGuideNote_1.0"
)
stopifnot(identical(unname(object_counts[expected_ids]), c(1L, 2L, 2L)))
```

The RDS payload has `__object__` for the saved root and `__robjc__` for class
metadata. The counts show one notebook, two sections, and two *distinct* notes.
The metadata may also contain ancestor classes with no direct instances.
Direct `readRDS()` is useful for inspection; use `robjc_read_rds()` to resolve
class references before working with the object.

## Restore with the current classes

The reader needs a map from each saved custom class ID to its current class
generator. In a new R session, define or load all three classes first, then
build the map. `RSWrappedClass` constructs the name-and-version ID for each
generator; those IDs become the dictionary keys. The package's standard
classes are mapped automatically.

```{r}
# Restore procedure: map each custom class ID to a current class definition.
wrapped_classes <- lapply(list(Notebook, Section, Note), RSWrappedClass$new)
class_map <- RSDictionary_withObjectsForKeys(
  objects = wrapped_classes,
  keys = lapply(wrapped_classes, function(x) x$classID())
)

# Restore procedure: read the file and resolve the saved class references.
loaded <- robjc_read_rds(path, class_map = class_map)

# Verification only: check classes, atomic fields, and the shared Note identity.
stopifnot(identical(loaded$class(), Notebook))
stopifnot(identical(loaded$sections[[1]]$class(), Section))
stopifnot(identical(loaded$sections[[1]]$notes[[1]]$class(), Note))
stopifnot(identical(loaded$sections[[1]]$name, "Current"))
stopifnot(identical(loaded$sections[[1]]$notes[[2]]$title, "Draft outline"))
stopifnot(identical(loaded$sections[[1]]$notes[[1]]$priority, 2.5))
stopifnot(identical(loaded$sections[[1]]$notes[[1]]$tags, c("release", "shared")))
stopifnot(identical(
  loaded$sections[[1]]$notes[[1]],
  loaded$sections[[2]]$notes[[1]]
))

# Clean up this example's temporary file.
unlink(path)
```

The last check tests **object identity**, not just matching note text: both
sections refer to the same restored `Note` instance. Class resolution updates
the notebook, both sections, and both notes because each was registered during
encoding. The title, priority, tags, and section name were restored by R's
ordinary RDS serialization; they never appeared in `objectsForEncoding()`.

The saved class name and version must match the current class definition.
Class resolution updates the class reference and S3 class names; it does not
migrate fields or replace the methods already carried by a serialized R6
instance. For the underlying class table and traversal strategy, see
`vignette("robjc_encoding_strategy", package = "robjc")`.
